<reason>Both sides were excellent and fully format-compliant (proper Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure, no fake precision, crystallizing closings). A built a vivid, coherent case: the status quo is already captured, the vacuum polarizes, and only a paid watcher sits through the meeting. But B did more decisive damage. B's pandemic school-board counterexample — saturation local coverage that grew more tribal, not less — struck A's core depolarization mechanism, and A never squarely answered it, retreating to "a shared object is still better than none," which the example directly disputes. B's comparative framing ("funding had to beat zero-capture-risk substitutes, not the void") held A to the motion as written, and the foreclosure point (donors won't fund nonprofits against a government desk) went unanswered. Finally, A's clever closing trap — that CON needs the desk both distrusted and trust-conferring — was cleanly dissolved by B's in-group-legitimacy/out-group-grievance mechanism, the single strongest closing move of the debate. A's corruption case stayed live and its "darkness needs no statute" line landed, but more of A's case was damaged than B's.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's two-stage kill of A's polarization mechanism: the unanswered school-board counterexample (shared objects didn't depolarize), followed by the closing dissolution of A's contradiction trap — one desk certifies innocence for the majority while polarizing the minority, so capture and polarization run through a single mechanism rather than canceling out.</best_rebuttal>
